data.title: A metal-detector survey at a hillfort – working with archaeologists
data.excerpt: On Friday we went to help out with metal detectors at an official excavation of a hillfort in northern Slovakia. Among the finds were a great many medieval iron arrowheads, all of the same shape and all pointing the same way, which opens up an otherwise unrecorded story of a medieval battle for the hillfort.
data.metaTitle: A metal-detector survey at a hillfort
data.metaDescription: What metal detecting in cooperation with archaeologists can achieve: at an official excavation of a hillfort, a great many identically oriented medieval arrows.

children.text: On Friday we went to help out with metal detectors at an official excavation of one hillfort in northern Slovakia. This example shows how beneficial metal detecting in cooperation with archaeologists is. We found, for instance, a great many medieval iron arrowheads. All of them were oriented in the same direction and had the same shape. Thanks to precise surveying the archaeologist has their distribution across the area of the hillfort documented, and from that he can see that they were concentrated in a relatively small space, so it is possible to assume where the attackers were shooting from and what they concentrated their attack on. That in itself already reveals a hitherto unknown story of a medieval battle for the hillfort, which apparently took place here. And yet we have no written mentions of it preserved. The archaeologist will certainly write an interesting article about it. In this way we have contributed to the knowledge of Slovak history. If the same arrows had been found by looters, they would have thrown them into a bag, sold them off somewhere at a collectors’ fair for 10 euros apiece, and the whole story would have been lost for ever. That is another reason why metal detectors should be used to help, and not to do damage.
